Constructive Episodic Simulation (CES)

Constructive episodic simulation — episodic memory is adaptive and constructive; it recombines past fragments to imagine futures.

Constructive Episodic Simulation (CES) holds that episodic memory is not a literal replay but a flexible system that recombines elements of past episodes to construct vivid simulations of possible futures; this same flexibility that enables planning and problem‑solving also makes memory vulnerable to distortions and false details. The hypothesis is supported by convergent evidence that remembering and imagining recruit a shared core network (hippocampus, medial prefrontal, posterior cingulate/precuneus, lateral parietal), and that hippocampal damage impairs not only remembering but also future imagining. Behavioral studies show that engaging episodic future thinking can change decisions (e.g., reduce delay discounting) by making future outcomes more concrete.

Mechanism & brain networks

  • Fragment recombination. CES proposes that details (people, places, events) are flexibly recombined from memory to simulate novel scenarios.
  • Scene construction. The hippocampus helps build spatially coherent scenes into which details are inserted (“scene construction theory”).
  • Core/Default Mode Network. Remembering the past and imagining the future co‑activate a core DMN set (hippocampus, vmPFC, PCC/precuneus, lateral parietal).
  • Encoding simulations. Newly imagined scenes themselves can be encoded into memory, with right hippocampus tracking this process.

Benefits vs. distortion trade‑off

Flexibility yields benefits—planning, creativity, problem‑solving—but it introduces systematic vulnerabilities (misbinding, confabulation, gist‑based errors). CES frames such “sins” as adaptive by‑products of a system optimized for future use, not archival accuracy.

Decision making effect: When people vividly simulate personal future events during choices, they discount delayed rewards less steeply; neuroimaging suggests enhanced coupling among hippocampal–prefrontal valuation circuits.
